sections.what: Air Alliance Houston researches air pollution and supports communities exposed to industrial and transport emissions. It monitors local air and helps residents engage with permits, regulators and public planning. Its campaigns seek cleaner air and stronger protections for Houston-area neighborhoods.
sections.monitoring: The September 2026 monitoring report describes more than 100 sensors across ten communities. Weather and maintenance affect observed pollution patterns, and the report does not establish recipient-caused exposure reductions. Campaigns address industrial permits, port operations, transportation and chemical disasters; activity is not proof of policy enactment or implementation. The FY2025 annual report describes a cancelled EPA grant, which must not be treated as delivered monitoring capacity or completed emissions reductions. Useful follow-up would include permit conditions changed, enforcement dates, exposure changes, distinct affected residents and job/provider incidence. Neither Houston's population nor a sensor count is converted into measured QALYs.
sections.qualitative: Current monitoring provides neighborhood-scale pollution data. Permit participation links technical research with practical regulatory decisions. Campaigns identify concrete local sources and affected communities. Sensors and comments do not themselves prove exposure or health improvements. Coalition attribution and implementation remain uncertain and can take years. Compliance costs, displaced jobs and alternative regulatory action may offset benefits. The original return for the year ending June 2025 identifies Air Alliance Houston, EIN 76-0461030. The current official giving page links secure.airalliancehouston.org and EveryAction. No transaction was performed. Local coalition participation does not establish attribution of all national regulatory benefits.
sections.cost: Our conditional reference is approximately $21.37 million per better life: ten combined healthy-year welfare equivalents. It combines 1.147147 clinical QALYs with 0.067097 signed income/consumption equivalents against a full annual recognized recipient cost of $2,594,790. A proportional $10,000 share corresponds to approximately 0.004680 combined equivalents under annual accounting, not demonstrated next-gift response. We assume 10,000 distinct resident opportunities in one annual permit/mitigation channel; this is a judgment, not a measured beneficiary cohort. An additional policy-change probability of 0.3, implementation probability of 0.5 and recipient causal attribution of 0.2 produce a single combined factor of 0.03. EPA, TCEQ, industry compliance and other coalition actors remain in the counterfactual. The resulting 300 exposed resident proxies contain 150 clinical responders under a 0.5 clinical response assumption. Utility improvement of 0.003 lasts three finite years, discounted at 3% after a two-year implementation delay; full union harm is 0.0001, and a Houston share of 0.95 is applied once. These are unsupported causal priors, not mortality estimates inferred from sensors. Half of exposed residents are assumed to avoid $100 of actual medical or foregone-work costs, net of insurance, benefits and replacement support. A 0.5 positive-only overlap adjustment is applied before the full $10 access/process burden, leaving $40 for successful residents and −$10 for the rest. One adult consumption-equivalent at a $30,000 annual baseline enters a joint resource logarithm. The resource gain lasts one year, not three repeated clinical-benefit years. Financial-only, negative job/compliance, failed-policy burden, weak-attribution, implementation-delay and payer/provider-loss cases preserve full negative gains, unavoidable costs and union harms. Central job loss and outside incidence are unknown-neutral assumptions, not observed zero effects. The whole annual recipient cost covers education, monitoring and other campaigns, while this narrow hypothetical channel does not capture complete portfolio expected value or establish a marginal donation offer. Public enforcement, partner labor, employer compliance, energy costs and displaced jobs require separate opportunity-cost assessment; transfers and avoided provider bills are not automatically new world resources.
sections.funding: The latest original return covers July 2024–June 2025: $2,588,981 of functional expenses plus $5,809 of direct event expenses netted from revenue gives $2,594,790. The years ending June 2024 and June 2023 report $3,200,249 and $2,785,438, with unpopulated direct-event expense lines. FY2025 education expense of $1,524,341 and air-quality advocacy expense of $180,396 are activity costs, not measured health returns. The annual report records the cancellation of an EPA grant; its intended funding cannot be counted as delivered capacity. The conditional benefits are finite future effects attributed to one annual work hypothesis, not perpetual policy credit.

model.formula: Union=N*unique*b; clinical=union*completion*q*discounted finite years minus full union harms. Financial=.5*people*discounted one-year log(1+joint net gain/baseline), local share once. Headline=10*C/(clinical+financial).
model.attribution: Annual incremental recipient response is distinct from cohort deduplication and geographic share; no claim of whole annual portfolio or marginal donation causal effect.
model.uncertainty: Source-grounded original cost/services; all causal mapping, utility and net resource priors unsupported. Complete portfolio and marginal donor EV unknown.
